passage: I'm Pema. For a whole term of swimming lessons, I pretended I could float. I'd hang on to the side and kick, and when the teacher looked, I'd bob my head under as if I'd just come up. I thought if I said I couldn't, everyone would laugh. In the holidays my cousin Hemant took me to the lake. I watched him float on his back like it was nothing, and my throat went tight. Then I said it: “I need help. I can't float.” He didn't laugh. He put one hand under my back and said, “Breathe in big. Now let go.” By the third day, I floated alone. I wish I'd asked in the first week.

qa.q: Where did Hemant take Pema?
qa.a: Hemant took Pema to the lake.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling during the term of pretending?
qa.a: Pema felt afraid of being laughed at and ashamed of not being able to float, so kept pretending.

qa.q: Why was saying “I need help” a strength for Pema?
qa.a: It got Pema real help from someone trusted, and within three days Pema could float alone.

qa.q: How did Hemant respond to Pema's request?
qa.a: Hemant didn't laugh; he supported Pema's back and gave simple instructions until Pema could float.

grounding: Shows a child who feared being judged finally saying I need help to a trusted person, and asking turning out to be a strength.

passage: Teacher's note, Monday. Nilesh, Class 4. Abhinav never asks for help. For two weeks he has handed in fraction sheets with the hard half blank, and when I ask, he says, “I forgot.” Today I watched him stare at question six for ten minutes, pencil still, cheeks red, glancing at the others. I think he's scared of looking slow in front of them. So I've put a small tin of green cards on each table. Put one on your desk if you're stuck, and I'll come over quietly. No hands up, no announcements. Within twenty minutes, Abhinav's green card was out. We worked through question six together, in whispers.

qa.q: What did Nilesh put on each table?
qa.a: Nilesh put a small tin of green cards on each table.

qa.q: What was Abhinav likely feeling as he stared at question six?
qa.a: Abhinav was likely stuck and scared of looking slow in front of the others, his cheeks going red.

qa.q: Why did the green cards help Abhinav ask for help?
qa.a: They made asking private, with no hands up or announcements, so he could ask without fearing judgement.

qa.q: What would change if Nilesh had asked Abhinav in front of the class why he was stuck?
qa.a: Abhinav would probably have felt more exposed and ashamed, and might have kept hiding that he needed help.

grounding: Shows a child who never asks for help because he fears judgement, and a teacher building a safe way to ask.

passage: Thursday. Aditi's diary. I lost my bus pass today. I searched my bag three times and felt sick. First I asked Yash, and he just said, “Uh-oh, you'll have to walk,” which didn't help at all. Then I thought, who would actually know what to do? Not Yash. Not the bus driver; he's always grumpy. The school office. I made myself walk in and say, “I need help. I've lost my bus pass.” The lady there didn't even look surprised. She phoned the transport teacher, who wrote me a slip for today and said a new pass would come on Monday. Asking the right person took five minutes. Worrying took all morning.

qa.q: When will the new bus pass come?
qa.a: The new pass will come on Monday.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling after searching the bag three times?
qa.a: Aditi felt sick with worry about losing the bus pass.

qa.q: How did Aditi decide who to ask for help?
qa.a: Aditi thought about who would actually know what to do and chose the school office instead of Yash or the bus driver.

qa.q: Why was Yash's reply not much help?
qa.a: Yash only pointed out the problem, saying Aditi would have to walk, without knowing how to fix it.

grounding: Shows a child saying I need help and choosing the right person to ask.

passage: Saturday: “Mummy, can I cycle to the market alone?” Jomon asked. Rehana shook her head. “Not yet. The main road has trucks, and you've never crossed it on your own. That's the reason, not that I don't trust you.” Jomon kicked the doorstep, but he understood about the trucks. Monday: They cycled the route together after school. Rehana showed him where to get off and walk the bike across, and where to wait. Wednesday: “Can I go to Joseph Uncle's shop for bread? It's before the main road.” Rehana thought. “Yes. Straight there, straight back, and ring the bell when you're home.” Jomon was back in twelve minutes, ringing the bell twice.

qa.q: What was Jomon allowed to fetch on Wednesday?
qa.a: He was allowed to go to Joseph Uncle's shop for bread.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling when he kicked the doorstep?
qa.a: Jomon felt disappointed and frustrated at the no, though he understood the reason about the trucks.

qa.q: Why did Rehana's clear reason help Jomon accept the no?
qa.a: It showed the no was about safety on the main road, not distrust, and led to practice and a smaller yes.

qa.q: What might Rehana have felt when Jomon rang the bell twice?
qa.a: Rehana probably felt relieved and proud that he kept to the plan.

grounding: Shows a child asking permission and learning it depends on safety and trust, with a clear reason helping him accept a no.

passage: Manoj, you're angry I said no to the late film. Sit. Let your Kishore Thatha tell you about the Ther festival when I was eleven. The whole gang was walking across the river to see it at night. I asked my father, “Appa, may I go?” He said no. I shouted that he never trusted me. He waited until I stopped. Then he said, “It's not trust. The river rises fast in this season, and none of you can swim. At night, nobody would see you.” I sulked all evening. Two boys came back soaked and shivering; the water had risen to their chests. The next morning, Appa took me himself, by the bridge.

qa.q: Where was the Ther festival?
qa.a: The Ther festival was across the river.

qa.q: What was young Kishore feeling when his father said no?
qa.a: He felt angry and hurt, believing his father didn't trust him.

qa.q: What choice did his father make that helped Kishore accept the no?
qa.a: He waited for Kishore to finish shouting, gave the real reason about the fast-rising river and the dark, and later took him by the bridge.

qa.q: What was the night like for the two boys who went?
qa.a: They came back soaked and shivering after the river rose to their chests, which showed the danger was real.

grounding: Shows a child asking may I go and learning that permission depends on safety, with a clear reason helping him accept the no.

passage: Alka was already late, keys in one hand, bag slipping off her shoulder, when Lakshmi ran after her down the stairs. “Masi, can I sleep over at Esha's tonight? Please? Everyone's going!” Alka stopped on the landing. There was no time for a long talk. “Not tonight, sweetheart. Here's why: I haven't met Esha's parents yet, and I don't know who else will be there. That's the only reason.” Lakshmi's face crumpled. “But—” “Tonight, ask Esha if her mum can call me. If we talk, next time might be a yes.” Lakshmi nodded, still disappointed. That evening, Esha's mother called. Alka liked her. The next sleepover was a yes.

qa.q: Why did Alka say no to the sleepover?
qa.a: She hadn't met Esha's parents yet and didn't know who else would be there.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi feeling when her face crumpled?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt disappointed and left out, since everyone else was going.

qa.q: How did Alka give a clear reason despite being rushed?
qa.a: She stopped briefly, said exactly why it was a no and gave Lakshmi a step, a phone call, that could lead to a yes next time.

qa.q: What made Alka comfortable saying yes the next time?
qa.a: Talking to Esha's mother on the phone helped Alka trust the plan, so she felt comfortable saying yes.

grounding: Shows a child asking permission and a rushed adult giving a clear reason for the no based on safety and trust.

passage: In the courtyard of their Mumbai building, Gargi was organising a play for the Diwali function. “You! Stand there. No, THERE. Tanay, stop smiling. Everyone, say your lines louder!” Three of the younger kids were already drifting towards the swings. Francis Uncle, who lived on the ground floor and had once directed plays at his college, called her over. “You've got good ideas,” he said. “But you sound exactly like a strict teacher.” Gargi's face fell. “If I don't tell them, it'll be a mess, and the show's on Saturday.” “So you're worried. Try, ‘How about we…?’” Gargi went back. “How about we try the song first?” The kids came back from the swings.

qa.q: When was the show?
qa.a: The show was on Saturday.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling behind all the commands?
qa.a: Gargi was worried the play would be a mess before Saturday, so the bossiness came from anxiety as well as leadership.

qa.q: What did Francis Uncle suggest, and why did it work?
qa.a: He suggested “How about we…?”, which turned commands into invitations, and the kids came back from the swings.

qa.q: What was the rehearsal like for the younger kids?
qa.a: They felt bossed around and drifted off to the swings, not enjoying being ordered about.

grounding: Shows a child's bossy commands coming from leadership and worry, and an adult coaching her to use invitations like how about we.

passage: “Move your piece there. No, THERE! Because I said so!” Aadhya jabbed at the board. Her little cousin pulled his hand back. “You're not the boss of the game.” Vandana looked up from her sewing. “Aadhya, come here a sec.” “What?” “‘Because I said so.’ Where have you heard that?” Aadhya went pink. “You. When I don't want to do homework.” Vandana laughed. “Fair. It doesn't work on you either, does it?” “No.” “So try asking. ‘Do you want to go there? It gets you closer.’” Aadhya went back. “Do you want to move there? It's a shortcut.” Her cousin looked. “Oh. Okay!” They played until dinner.

qa.q: Where had Aadhya heard “Because I said so”?
qa.a: Aadhya had heard it from Vandana, when Aadhya didn't want to do homework.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling when Vandana asked where she'd heard it?
qa.a: Aadhya felt embarrassed, going pink, realising she was copying Vandana's tone.

qa.q: What did Vandana coach Aadhya to say instead?
qa.a: She coached her to ask and give a reason, like “Do you want to move there? It's a shortcut,” instead of ordering.

qa.q: How did the little cousin feel about being ordered?
qa.a: He felt bossed and pulled his hand back, saying Aadhya wasn't the boss of the game.

grounding: Shows a child's bossy commands copying an adult's tone, and the adult coaching her to invite instead.

passage: I'm Arnab. When I was made captain of our under-eleven cricket team last year, I thought captains were supposed to shout. “Field there! Bowl faster! Don't drop it!” My dad shouts like that at the TV, and it sounded like leading. By the third match, Abhinav, my best friend, stopped talking to me. After the game he said, “You're not a captain, you're a sergeant.” That stung. That night I thought about the captains I actually liked, and none of them shouted. At the next practice I tried, “How about we move you to slip? You've got quick hands.” Abhinav grinned and went. We won that match by four wickets.

qa.q: By how many wickets did they win the match?
qa.a: They won by four wickets.

qa.q: How did Arnab feel when Abhinav used the word sergeant?
qa.a: Arnab felt stung and hurt, realising the shouting was pushing a best friend away.

qa.q: What did Arnab change, and why did it work?
qa.a: Arnab swapped commands for invitations with a reason, like “How about we move you to slip?”, which made teammates want to follow.

qa.q: What was the season like for Abhinav before the change?
qa.a: Abhinav felt ordered about and upset enough to stop talking to his best friend.

grounding: Shows a child's commands copying an adult's tone, and the child learning to swap them for invitations like how about we.

passage: Monday: Karthik was drawing a dragon for the art contest. Lalremsiami leaned over. “The wings are too small. And you should use red, not green.” Karthik covered the page with his arm. “I didn't ask.” Wednesday: Lalremsiami told her mother about it, still annoyed. “I was helping!” Her mother said, “Were you? Or were you telling? Next time, ask if he wants ideas.” Friday: Karthik was stuck on the dragon's tail, rubbing it out again and again. Lalremsiami sat on her hands for a moment. Then she said, “Would you like an idea, or do you want to figure it out?” Karthik looked up. “…An idea.” She suggested a curl like a question mark. He tried it and grinned.

qa.q: What was Karthik drawing?
qa.a: Karthik was drawing a dragon for the art contest.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling when he covered the page with his arm?
qa.a: Karthik felt annoyed and a bit hurt that his drawing was being criticised when he hadn't asked.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami change on Friday, and why did it work?
qa.a: She asked whether he wanted an idea before giving one, so the advice felt like help, not bossiness.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami's mother see Monday's advice?
qa.a: Her mother saw it as telling rather than helping, and suggested asking first.

grounding: Shows a child's unasked-for advice feeling bossy, and asking would you like an idea making it kind.

passage: Yogesh, your friend didn't ask how to fix his bike, did he? Let your Devika Dadi tell you about Kamla. When I was ten, Kamla was my best friend, and I was very clever, I thought. I told her how to plait her hair, how to hold her pen, how to talk to her brother. I thought I was helping. One day she said, “Devika, you're like a second mother. I already have one.” She walked home with another girl for a week. I was miserable. Then I went to her and said, “I'm sorry. From now on, I'll ask if you want my ideas.” She laughed and said, “Sometimes I will.” We were friends for sixty years.

qa.q: What did Kamla call young Devika?
qa.a: Kamla said Devika was like a second mother.

qa.q: What was young Devika feeling during the week Kamla walked with another girl?
qa.a: She felt miserable and lonely, missing her best friend.

qa.q: What choice did Devika make to repair the friendship?
qa.a: She apologised and promised to ask Kamla whether she wanted ideas before giving advice.

qa.q: What was all the advice like for Kamla?
qa.a: Kamla felt bossed and smothered, as if she had a second mother telling her what to do.

grounding: Shows a child's constant unasked-for advice feeling bossy to a friend, and learning to ask whether ideas are wanted.

passage: The group project was due in an hour, the printer was jammed, and Rashmi was trying to fit five pictures onto one chart, sighing. Chetan could see exactly how to fix it: two rows, not one long line. The words were almost out of his mouth. But last week, when he'd told Pihu how to do her poster, she'd snapped, “I didn't ask!” So he stopped himself. “Rashmi, would you like an idea for the pictures, or are you okay?” Rashmi didn't look up. “Give me two minutes to try.” Chetan waited, fiddling with the stapler. After two minutes she groaned. “Okay. Idea, please.” “Two rows?” She tried it. It fit perfectly.

qa.q: How long was left before the project was due?
qa.a: The project was due in an hour.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling as he waited, fiddling with the stapler?
qa.a: Chetan felt impatient and eager to help, but held back to respect Rashmi's wish to try first.

qa.q: Why was asking “would you like an idea” better than telling?
qa.a: It let Rashmi choose, so she tried first and then asked for help, making the advice welcome rather than bossy.

qa.q: What was the hour like for Rashmi?
qa.a: Rashmi was stressed and frustrated, trying to fit five pictures onto one chart with the printer jammed.

grounding: Shows a child holding back unasked-for advice under time pressure and asking would you like an idea first.

passage: At the swimming club, everyone changed in one big room, and Anirban hated it. On his third Saturday he stood outside the door, towel clutched to his chest, until the others had gone in. Then he found Coach Sangeeta. “Ma'am, can I change somewhere by myself? I don't like changing in front of people.” She didn't laugh or ask why. “Of course. The small room next to the office has a lock. Use it every time.” Then she added, “One rule: always tell me or the desk you're going in there, so an adult knows where you are.” Anirban nodded. The next Saturday he walked in whistling.

qa.q: Which room did Coach Sangeeta offer Anirban?
qa.a: She offered the small room next to the office, which has a lock.

qa.q: What was Anirban feeling as he stood outside with his towel?
qa.a: Anirban felt uncomfortable and embarrassed about changing in front of others.

qa.q: How did Coach Sangeeta honour Anirban's request and keep him safe?
qa.a: She gave him a private room with a lock and set one rule: always tell an adult he's going in there, so someone knows where he is.

qa.q: How might Coach Sangeeta see Anirban's request?
qa.a: She treated it as a normal, reasonable wish for privacy, without laughing or asking why.

grounding: Shows a child asking for privacy while changing, and an adult honouring it while explaining a safety limit.

passage: I'm Arnab, and my big sister Nazia keeps a diary with a little lock. Last week Mummy found it lying open on the sofa and picked it up to close it. Nazia ran in, red-faced. “Please don't read it! It's private.” I thought there'd be a fight. Instead Mummy handed it straight back. “I wasn't reading. Your diary is yours.” Then she sat down. “But if something ever feels unsafe, or someone is hurting you, that's not a diary secret. Tell me.” Nazia nodded and hugged the diary. I don't know what's in it. I think Nazia trusts Mummy more now, though.

qa.q: What does Nazia's diary have?
qa.a: Nazia's diary has a little lock.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling when she ran in, red-faced?
qa.a: Nazia felt alarmed and embarrassed that her private diary might be read.

qa.q: How did Mummy honour Nazia's privacy and still set a safety limit?
qa.a: She handed the diary back unread and said it was Nazia's, but explained that anything unsafe or anyone hurting her is not a diary secret.

qa.q: How does Arnab think the moment changed things?
qa.a: Arnab thinks Nazia trusts Mummy more after seeing her privacy respected.

grounding: Shows a child asking for privacy with a diary, and a parent honouring it while explaining that safety concerns must be shared.

passage: Monday: Bhavna was in the bathroom when her little brother barged in looking for his toy boat. “GET OUT!” she screamed. He cried. Rekha came running. Tuesday: At bedtime Bhavna said, quietly this time, “Amma, I need the bathroom to be private. Can there be a knocking rule?” Rekha nodded. “That's fair. You're growing up. Everyone knocks, even me. But don't slide the top bolt, so if you ever slip, I can get in.” Thursday: A tiny knock came at the bathroom door. “Didi? Is my boat in there?” Bhavna laughed. “Wait two minutes!” She handed it out, dripping, through the gap.

qa.q: What was Bhavna's brother looking for?
qa.a: He was looking for his toy boat.

qa.q: What was Bhavna feeling when she screamed “GET OUT”?
qa.a: Bhavna felt shocked and embarrassed at her privacy being broken.

qa.q: How did Rekha honour Bhavna's request and keep a safety limit?
qa.a: She made a knocking rule for everyone but asked Bhavna not to slide the top bolt, so Rekha could get in if she ever slipped.

qa.q: What was Thursday like for Bhavna's little brother?
qa.a: He remembered to knock and got his boat back without any shouting.

grounding: Shows a child asking calmly for bathroom privacy, and a parent honouring it with a knocking rule and a safety limit.

passage: I'm Vikas. On Monday, Sir told Class 5 we couldn't use the big playground at break any more. Everyone groaned. Siddharth stood up. I thought he'd shout, like he does at cricket. Instead he said, “Sir, that feels unfair. Class 6 still uses it. Can you tell us why?” Sir didn't get angry. “Fair question. They're digging for the new water tank near the swings, and your break is when the trucks come in. Class 6 has break after the trucks leave.” Siddharth thought. “Then can we have the small ground instead?” “Yes. That I can do.” The big playground stayed a no. I don't know what Siddharth felt, but he sat down calm.

qa.q: What was being dug near the swings?
qa.a: They were digging for the new water tank near the swings.

qa.q: What was Siddharth likely feeling when he stood up?
qa.a: Siddharth was likely frustrated and felt the rule was unfair, since Class 6 still used the playground.

qa.q: How did Siddharth object in a way that worked?
qa.a: He said calmly that it felt unfair, asked for the reason, then suggested an alternative, the small ground.

qa.q: How did Sir respond to being questioned?
qa.a: Sir called it a fair question, explained the safety reason about the trucks and agreed to the small ground while keeping the no.

grounding: Shows a child objecting to a rule with respectful words, understanding the safety reason, and an adult supporting the objection though the answer stays no.

passage: Friday: Papa said Charu couldn't watch the horror film with her cousins. “NOT FAIR!” she yelled, and slammed her door. Papa didn't come after her. Saturday: Charu wrote a note and slid it under the study door: Papa, everyone else is watching it. Please explain why not. Sachin, her Papa, read it and came out. “Thank you for writing, not yelling. The last scary film gave you nightmares for a week, and you slept in our bed. That's why.” Charu remembered. “It's still a no?” “It's still a no. But you pick the next film for everyone.” Sunday: Charu picked a comedy. Even the cousins laughed.

qa.q: What gave Charu nightmares for a week?
qa.a: The last scary film gave her nightmares for a week.

qa.q: What was Charu feeling when she yelled “NOT FAIR”?
qa.a: Charu felt angry and left out, since her cousins were all watching the film.

qa.q: How did Charu's objection change from Friday to Saturday?
qa.a: She moved from yelling and slamming the door to writing a respectful note asking for the reason.

qa.q: How did Sachin respond to the note?
qa.a: Sachin thanked her for writing instead of yelling, explained the reason, kept the no and let her choose the next film.

grounding: Shows a child learning to object with respectful words, and a parent supporting that even when the answer stays no.

passage: Keerthana, you were right to tell the coach it wasn't fair. Let your Jaya Paati tell you about my science club. When I was twelve, our headmaster made a rule: only boys could join, because girls might break the glass tubes. I was so angry I wanted to throw a tube myself. Instead, my mother helped me write a letter. I took it to his office and said, “Sir, I respectfully object. I've never broken anything. Please let me try for one month.” He looked at me over his spectacles for a long time. Then he said, “One month.” I didn't break a single tube. By the next year, six girls had joined.

qa.q: How long did the headmaster first let Jaya try?
qa.a: He let her try for one month.

qa.q: What was young Jaya feeling about the boys-only rule?
qa.a: She felt angry at the unfairness, so angry she wanted to throw a tube herself.

qa.q: What choice did young Jaya make, and why did it work?
qa.a: She wrote a letter and objected respectfully in person, asking for a fair trial, which the headmaster granted.

qa.q: What might the headmaster have thought as he looked over his spectacles?
qa.a: He may have been surprised by her calm, respectful objection and decided it deserved a fair chance.

grounding: Shows a child objecting to unfair treatment with respectful words, supported by an adult.

passage: Friday. Asif's diary. Abbu promised last week, “I'll be at your race, no matter what.” This morning he called from the office. His voice was sad. “Beta, the machine at work broke and I'm the only one who can fix it. I can't come. I'm really sorry. I know I promised.” I felt like someone had let the air out of me. I said, “You PROMISED,” and hung up. Then I felt bad. At the race, Gurpreet's mum filmed me running, for Abbu. I came second. Tonight Abbu watched the video three times and said, “Next time I promise, I'll only promise what I can control.” That made it a bit better.

qa.q: Why couldn't Abbu come to the race?
qa.a: The machine at work broke, and he was the only one who could fix it.

qa.q: What was Asif feeling when Abbu said he couldn't come?
qa.a: Asif felt deflated and hurt, as if the air had been let out, because Abbu had promised.

qa.q: How did Abbu handle the broken promise?
qa.a: He called beforehand, explained honestly and said sorry, then watched the video and promised to only promise what he can control.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet's mum help?
qa.a: She filmed Asif's race so Abbu could still see it, which softened the disappointment.

grounding: Shows a child treating a parent's broken promise as a serious hurt, and honest explanation helping rebuild trust.

passage: Before leaving for the district town, Rekha knelt in the courtyard and held Yamini's hands. “I promise I'll be back before dark to see your dance at the school function.” Yamini had heard promises before, from other grown-ups. That afternoon the rain came down in sheets, and the last bus from town was cancelled. Yamini stood at the school gate in her costume, watching the empty road. The function began. Her turn came closer. Then, just as her music started, a figure came splashing up the path, sari soaked to the knees, chappals in one hand. Rekha had walked four kilometres. She stood at the back, dripping, and waved. Yamini danced better than she ever had.

qa.q: How far did Rekha walk?
qa.a: Rekha walked four kilometres.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling as she watched the empty road?
qa.a: Yamini felt anxious and doubtful, afraid the promise would be broken like other grown-ups' promises before.

qa.q: Why did Rekha's kept promise matter so much?
qa.a: Keeping it despite the rain and cancelled bus showed Yamini her mother's word could be trusted.

qa.q: What might the walk have been like for Rekha?
qa.a: It was probably wet and exhausting, but she was determined to keep her promise to Yamini.

grounding: Shows a child hearing a parent's pledge and a kept promise building trust.

passage: In their Stockholm flat, Astrid had promised Kaito a trip north to see the northern lights in the winter holiday. He'd drawn them on every page of his notebook. Two days before, she sat on his bed. “Kaito, I have to tell you something honestly. My work has changed my holiday, and we can't go this year. I'm really sorry. I know I promised.” Kaito turned to the wall. “You always say sorry.” Astrid didn't argue. “You're right to be upset. A promise is serious.” She took out the calendar. “February, the weekend after your birthday. I've already asked for the days off. It's written here, in pen.” Kaito looked at the pen mark for a long time, then nodded.

qa.q: When is the new trip planned?
qa.a: It's planned for February, the weekend after Kaito's birthday.

qa.q: What was Kaito feeling when he turned to the wall?
qa.a: Kaito felt hurt and let down, because he had been dreaming of the trip and a promise was broken.

qa.q: How did Astrid handle breaking the promise?
qa.a: She told him honestly and early, accepted his upset and made a specific new plan with the days already booked.

qa.q: What might Astrid have felt telling Kaito?
qa.a: Astrid probably felt guilty and sad, knowing how much the trip meant to him.

grounding: Shows a child treating a parent's broken promise as a serious hurt, and honest explanation and a firm new plan rebuilding trust.

passage: I'm Tushar. Last summer I announced at dinner, “I'm going to practise cricket every single day and be the best bowler in the colony.” Everyone clapped. I practised on Monday. On Tuesday it rained. By Friday I'd forgotten. My uncle Kishore didn't tease me. He said, “Big plan, no steps. Try this: twenty balls at one stump, after school, Monday, Wednesday and Friday. Mark them on the calendar.” It sounded too small. But I did it. After a month I could hit the stump eight times out of twenty. I didn't become the best bowler in the colony. I did become better than I was.

qa.q: How many balls did Kishore suggest Tushar bowl each time?
qa.a: He suggested twenty balls at one stump.

qa.q: How did Tushar feel when the family clapped at dinner?
qa.a: Tushar felt proud and excited about the big plan.

qa.q: Why did Kishore's plan work better than the first declaration?
qa.a: It was small and specific, with a set number, set days and a calendar, so Tushar could actually keep it up.

qa.q: How did Kishore react when the first plan fell apart?
qa.a: Kishore didn't tease; he calmly pointed out the plan had no steps and offered a smaller one.

grounding: Shows a child's big, vague declaration fading and a small, specific plan succeeding.

passage: Library note, Monday. Jomon, Class 4 teacher. Zeenat announced to the class today, “This year I'm going to read a hundred books!” The class was impressed. I've heard this from other children, and usually it fades by the second week. So at break I asked her, “What's the first step?” She looked puzzled. “Read… a lot?” We made it smaller together: two chapters every night before brushing her teeth, ticked on a chart stuck to her cupboard. She chose the first book herself. I'll check the chart with her every Monday. A hundred books is a wonderful dream. Two chapters tonight is a plan.

qa.q: Where is Zeenat's chart stuck?
qa.a: The chart is stuck to her cupboard.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling when asked about the first step?
qa.a: Zeenat felt puzzled, since she hadn't thought beyond the big, exciting goal.

qa.q: What small, specific plan did Jomon help Zeenat make?
qa.a: Two chapters every night before brushing her teeth, ticked on a chart, with a check every Monday.

qa.q: How did the class react to Zeenat's announcement?
qa.a: The class was impressed by the idea of reading a hundred books.

grounding: Shows a child declaring a big goal and a teacher helping turn it into a small, specific plan.

passage: Sunday. Elizabeth's diary. I've decided: I'm going to be amazing at the keyboard by Christmas. I told Arohi on the phone, and she said, “That's what you said about skating.” Rude. But true. I quit skating after three days. So this time I'm writing it smaller, here, so I have to see it. Plan: ten minutes every day after tea. Monday to Friday, scales. Saturday, one new song. Sunday, off. A sticker on the calendar for every day I do it. Arohi said she'll ask me every Friday how many stickers I have. Today was Sunday, so no practice. Tomorrow: ten minutes. That's all.

qa.q: When will Elizabeth practise each day?
qa.a: Elizabeth will practise for ten minutes every day after tea.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth feeling when Arohi mentioned skating?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt a little stung and annoyed at first, but admitted Arohi was right.

qa.q: Why is Elizabeth's new plan more likely to work?
qa.a: It is small and specific, with set times, tasks for each day, stickers and a Friday check-in with Arohi.

qa.q: How is Arohi helping Elizabeth keep the plan?
qa.a: Arohi will ask every Friday how many stickers Elizabeth has, keeping the plan honest.

grounding: Shows a child moving from a big, vague declaration to a small, specific practice plan.

passage: In the Lisbon school canteen, Abebe sat alone every day with his injera wrapped in foil. On Thursday, two boys walked past and held their noses. Paulo, at the next table, watched Abebe's shoulders curl. He picked up his tray and sat down opposite him. “What's that? It looks like a pancake.” Abebe blinked, then tore off a piece. “Injera. Try.” Paulo did. “It's sour! I like it.” When the two boys came back and started again, Paulo stood up. “Stop it. It's just food.” Then he walked to the lunch supervisor and told her. She came over, spoke to the boys and later told Paulo, “That was brave, and telling me was the right move.”

qa.q: What was Abebe's lunch wrapped in?
qa.a: His injera was wrapped in foil.

qa.q: What was Abebe feeling when the boys held their noses?
qa.a: Abebe felt hurt and embarrassed, his shoulders curling as they mocked his food.

qa.q: Which of Paulo's actions showed solidarity, and why was telling the supervisor right?
qa.a: Sitting with Abebe and standing up to the boys showed care, and telling the supervisor brought in an adult who could stop the teasing.

qa.q: How did the lunch supervisor respond?
qa.a: She spoke to the boys and praised Paulo for being brave and for telling her.

grounding: Shows a child sitting with a lonely classmate and standing up for him, and involving an adult, which the adult praises.

passage: In the first week at the residential school, Jyoti sat alone on the dining-hall steps every evening, not eating. Siddharth noticed on Monday, and again on Tuesday. On Wednesday he brought two bananas and sat a step below her. “Want one?” She shook her head, then took it. They didn't talk much. He told her about the hostel cat, and she almost smiled. On Thursday she still hadn't eaten dinner. Siddharth felt uneasy. This was more than he could fix with bananas. He went to the house warden and told her. The warden thanked him, sat with Jyoti that evening and called her parents. Later she told Siddharth, “You were a good friend, twice.”

qa.q: What did Siddharth bring on Wednesday?
qa.a: Siddharth brought two bananas.

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling when Jyoti still hadn't eaten on Thursday?
qa.a: Siddharth felt uneasy and worried, sensing the problem was bigger than he could fix alone.

qa.q: Why was going to the warden the right step?
qa.a: Jyoti not eating for days needed an adult's help, and the warden sat with her and called her parents that evening.

qa.q: What did the warden mean by “a good friend, twice”?
qa.a: The warden meant Siddharth helped once by sitting with Jyoti and again by telling an adult when it became serious.

grounding: Shows a child sitting with a lonely classmate and knowing when to involve an adult, with the adult praising both.

passage: I'm Charu. At the bus stop on Friday, two older boys started shoving Kunal, snatching his cap and throwing it between them. Kunal's face went white. Most of us looked away. Vijay didn't. He walked right up, not fast, and stood next to Kunal. “Give it back. Come on, Kunal, stand with me.” The older boys laughed but tossed the cap on the ground. Then Vijay did something I didn't expect: he didn't shout or push. He took Kunal straight to the teacher on bus duty and told her everything. She wrote down the boys' names and called both their homes that evening. I don't know what Vijay was feeling. His hands were shaking a bit.

qa.q: What did the older boys snatch from Kunal?
qa.a: They snatched Kunal's cap.

qa.q: What might Vijay have been feeling as he stood next to Kunal?
qa.a: Vijay was probably scared, his hands shaking a bit, but determined to stand up for his friend.

qa.q: What made Vijay's response safe and wise?
qa.a: He stood beside Kunal without fighting, then took him straight to the teacher on duty, who acted that evening.

qa.q: How did most of the other children react?
qa.a: Most of them, Charu included, looked away, which made Vijay's step stand out.

grounding: Shows a child standing up for a friend and involving an adult when the situation is unsafe.

passage: Camp leader's note, night two. Vinita, Group C. Rashmi was quiet at dinner and left most of her khichdi. At campfire she sat at the edge, hugging the knitted elephant her Nani made. When I sat beside her, she whispered, “I miss Mummy. I want to go home.” I told her missing home means she has people she loves, and that lots of campers feel it on the second night. We made a plan: she keeps the elephant by her pillow, and tomorrow at seven she calls home from my phone. I checked on her at lights-out. She was asleep, the elephant under her chin.

qa.q: Who made Rashmi's knitted elephant?
qa.a: Her Nani made the knitted elephant.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling as she hugged the elephant at the campfire?
qa.a: Rashmi felt homesick and sad, missing her mother and wanting to go home.

qa.q: What steps did Vinita take to help Rashmi?
qa.a: She listened, said missing home shows love, kept the elephant by her pillow, planned a call home at seven and checked on her at lights-out.

qa.q: Why might Vinita say missing home means having people you love?
qa.a: Vinita wanted Rashmi to see homesickness as a sign of healthy attachment, not something to be ashamed of.

grounding: Shows a child's homesickness at camp and how talking, a comfort item and a planned call help.

passage: Tuesday night. Ankita's diary. My third night at Nani's in the village. The days are fun: the calves, the mango tree, the pond. But at night I miss Papa so much my chest hurts. I brought his old blue T-shirt to sleep in, and it still smells a bit like him. Nani saw me crying and didn't say, “Don't be silly.” She said, “Missing someone means you love them. Shall we call him?” She dialled and called out, “Harish, your daughter wants you!” Papa told me the cat knocked over his tea. I laughed. We decided to call every night at eight. Only four more nights. The T-shirt helps.

qa.q: What did Ankita bring to sleep in?
qa.a: Ankita brought Papa's old blue T-shirt.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling at night at Nani's?
qa.a: Ankita felt homesick, missing Papa so much her chest hurt.

qa.q: What helped Ankita cope with missing Papa?
qa.a: Talking with Nani, the comfort of Papa's T-shirt and a planned call every night at eight.

qa.q: How did Nani respond to Ankita's tears?
qa.a: Nani didn't dismiss them; she said missing someone means you love them and offered to call Papa.

grounding: Shows a child's longing for a parent while away, and a comfort item, talking and planned calls helping.

passage: On the second evening of the school's village-stay camp, Shreya sat by the well while the others played kabaddi. She kept looking at the road. Her little brother Bhupen had cried when the bus left, and now she couldn't stop thinking about him: whether he'd found his torch, who was reading him his story. The teacher came and sat on the edge of the well. “Missing someone?” Shreya nodded. “My brother. He's scared of the dark.” “That's a big-sister feeling,” the teacher said. “Want to call him before his bedtime?” At eight, Shreya told Bhupen a story over the phone, from memory. Afterwards she went and joined the kabaddi game.

qa.q: What is Bhupen scared of?
qa.a: Bhupen is scared of the dark.

qa.q: What was Shreya feeling as she kept looking at the road?
qa.a: Shreya felt homesick and worried about her little brother, missing him and wondering who was reading his story.

qa.q: How did the teacher help Shreya?
qa.a: The teacher noticed, named the feeling kindly and offered a call before his bedtime, so she could tell him a story.

qa.q: How did Bhupen react when the bus left?
qa.a: Bhupen cried when the bus left, showing he missed his sister too.

grounding: Shows a child missing family at camp, and talking and a planned call helping her join in again.
